questions.question: How does the Fetch API send a request and read a response?
questions.title: Fetch Request and Response Flow
questions.direct_answer: `fetch(input, options)` starts an HTTP request and returns a Promise for a `Response` once status and headers are available. The response body is a stream read separately with an asynchronous method such as `json`, `text`, or `blob`; a body is normally consumed once, so choose or clone it deliberately.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand request options, the Response object, body consumption, parsing, and browser security boundaries.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating the `fetch` result as JSON or trying to consume one response body more than once.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the headers-then-body timeline and separate HTTP success from body-decoding success.

Configure method, headers, body, credentials, and signal through the options object.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`fetch(url, options)` starts an HTTP request and returns a Promise for a `Response`; it does not return parsed JSON. The Promise can fulfill as soon as status and headers are available, while body bytes may still be arriving. The Response therefore represents the HTTP envelope and gives code fields such as `status`, `ok`, and `headers`. The caller must still decide what that response means.

The options object contains the request method, headers, optional body, credentials policy, and abort signal. A JSON POST commonly uses `method: "POST"`, `body: JSON.stringify(data)`, and a matching `Content-Type: application/json` header. Those choices must follow the server's contract; fetch does not serialize an ordinary object body automatically.

Choose one body reader from the response format: `response.json()` for JSON, `text()` for text, or `blob()` for binary browser data. Each returns another Promise because reading and decoding the stream takes time. JSON parsing can fail even after a successful HTTP response when the body is empty or malformed.

A response body is normally consumed once, so a second call to `response.json()` or `response.text()` fails after the first reader finishes. Use `response.clone()` before either read only when two consumers genuinely need the body; cloning is not a default for large streams. Browser fetch also follows CORS rules, so client code cannot repair missing permission headers from the server.

sections.title: Concept: Fetch Request and Response Flow
sections.content:
**Two asynchronous stages.** Headers establish the `Response` object first. Body bytes can still be arriving, so decoding is another Promise-returning operation. Keeping these stages separate allows streaming and header-based decisions.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant App
  participant Fetch
  participant Server
  App->>Fetch: fetch(url, options)
  Fetch->>Server: HTTP request
  Server-->>Fetch: status + headers
  Fetch-->>App: fulfill with Response
  App->>Fetch: response.json()
  Fetch-->>App: parsed body or parse rejection
```

**Runnable example.** A data URL keeps the demonstration local while exercising the real Fetch and Response APIs in modern browsers and Node.

```javascript
const payload = encodeURIComponent(JSON.stringify({ id: 7, name: "Mina" }));
const response = await fetch("data:application/json," + payload);
console.log(response.ok, response.status); // true 200
const user = await response.json();
console.log(user.name); // Mina
console.log(response.bodyUsed); // true
```

**Boundary.** Browser fetch also obeys security rules such as CORS. A server may receive a request while browser JavaScript is still prevented from reading the response, so client code alone cannot repair missing server CORS headers.

questions.question: Why does `fetch` not reject for HTTP errors such as 404 or 500, and how should they be handled?
questions.title: Fetch HTTP Errors vs Network Errors
questions.direct_answer: Fetch normally fulfills with a `Response` when an HTTP server returns 404 or 500 because a valid HTTP response arrived. It rejects for failures that prevent a usable response, such as a network error, invalid scheme, or abort. Application code must check `response.ok` or `status`, then parse an error body according to the API contract.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you distinguish Fetch rejection from an HTTP error response and preserve body-decoding context.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using only `try/catch`, then treating a fulfilled 500 Response as successful data.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name transport, status, decoding, and schema validation as separate failure layers.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A 404 or 500 usually fulfills the Fetch Promise with `response.ok === false`.
`ok` is true for HTTP status codes in the 200–299 range.
Network failure, an invalid request URL or scheme, and abortion can reject the Fetch Promise.
Check status before treating the body as successful application data.
Body parsing has its own failure path and should match the declared content type.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A 404 or 500 means the server returned a valid HTTP response whose application result is unsuccessful. Because a usable `Response` arrived, the Promise from `fetch` normally fulfills. The response carries the status, and `response.ok` is `false`; `ok` is true only for status codes from 200 through 299. This preserves headers and an error body that may explain the server's decision.

Fetch rejects when it cannot produce a usable Response, for example because of a network failure, an unsupported URL scheme, cancellation, or some request-construction failures. A `try` and `catch` handles that rejection, but it does not automatically handle a fulfilled 500 Response. HTTP status needs its own explicit policy.

A helper should inspect `response.ok` or `response.status`, read an error body only in the format promised by the API, and preserve the status in the resulting error. The focused example reads text once, reports a 404 clearly, and returns `null` for an empty successful body instead of blindly calling `json()`.

A UI may turn a known 404 into “User not found,” show an offline message for a network rejection, and quietly ignore an intentional abort. A malformed success body is a decoding or contract problem, not another 404. Keeping transport, status, decoding, and validation separate gives accurate logs and lets each caller choose the right recovery.

questions.question: How do `AbortController`, request cancellation, and timeouts work with `fetch`?
questions.title: Cancelling Fetch Requests
questions.direct_answer: Pass an `AbortSignal` to `fetch`, then call its controller's `abort()` when the result is no longer needed. Fetch rejects with an abort-related error, and aborting after headers can also reject body consumption. A timeout is a policy built with an abort signal; cleanup must clear timers and ignore intentional aborts appropriately.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand controller-versus-signal roles, rejection behavior, timeout policy, and server-side limits.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Dropping an obsolete response in the UI without cancelling its work, or treating every abort as an offline error.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that cancellation can affect body consumption but cannot promise rollback of server work already performed.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Create an `AbortController` and pass `controller.signal` in Fetch options.
Calling `controller.abort()` notifies every operation using that signal.
Aborted Fetch work rejects; identify an abort separately from a real network failure.
A timeout is cancellation scheduled by policy, not a built-in HTTP status.
Clear timeout handles and abort obsolete UI requests during cleanup.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`AbortController` owns the cancellation action, while its `signal` carries that notification to fetch. Code creates a controller, passes `controller.signal` in the fetch options, and later calls `controller.abort()`. One signal may be shared deliberately by several operations that should be cancelled as a group. Otherwise, each independently owned request should normally have its own controller.

When fetch observes an abort, its Promise rejects with an abort-related reason instead of returning an HTTP status. If status and headers already produced a Response but the body has not finished, aborting can also make `response.json()` or another body reader reject. Intentional navigation cancellation should usually be handled differently from an offline error.

A timeout is not an HTTP status built into fetch; it is a policy that aborts waiting after a chosen duration. A wrapper can schedule `controller.abort()`, pass the signal to fetch, and clear the timer in `finally`. The caller can then translate that known abort into a timeout message when appropriate.

Cancellation is useful when a component unmounts, a search term changes, or a response is no longer needed. It stops the client from waiting and can save resources, but it cannot guarantee that a server undoes work already accepted, especially a write. Server-side idempotency and transaction rules protect that operation; AbortController only manages the client-side lifetime.
